h1: Belgian table beer and the low strength style made for long sessions
title: Belgian Table Beer: Low Strength Guide | Craft Beer School
desc: How to brew a Belgian table beer at 2.5 to 4% ABV that still tastes full, with grist, mash and yeast choices for homebrewers.
teaser: Belgium drank this beer with dinner for generations. Brewing it well at 3% is harder than brewing a tripel at 9%.
standfirst: Tafelbier, or table beer, is the everyday Belgian beer: light in alcohol, full of yeast character and meant for long meals. Making a small beer taste generous is the trick. This guide shows how a homebrewer can do it.
sections:
Belgian table beer, tafelbier in Flemish or bière de table in French, is a low strength beer for drinking with food. Traditionally it was the family beer, served with lunch and dinner. Modern versions sit around 2.5 to 4% ABV. They can be pale or dark and are often lightly sweet, with the fruity and spicy notes of a Belgian yeast.

Many farmhouse breweries made table beer as a smaller sibling of their saison. Abbey breweries brewed a light everyday beer for the monks too. The idea is the same: something easy to drink that still tastes like proper beer.

Alcohol carries flavour and gives body. Remove most of it and a beer can taste thin and watery. A big Belgian beer hides small mistakes under its strength. A table beer at 3% hides nothing.

The homebrewer's job is to put body and flavour back by other routes: a warmer mash, some specialty malt, a yeast with real character and the right carbonation. Each of these is a lever. The art is pulling them gently.

For 20 litres at an original gravity around 1.030 to 1.034, a starting point:

  • About 75% Pilsner malt as the base.
  • About 10% wheat malt or flaked oats for body and a soft head. Our guide on low alcohol craft beer explains why proteins and gums matter at this strength.
  • About 10% Munich or Vienna malt for bread and depth.
  • About 5% light caramel malt for a touch of sweetness.

That is roughly 3 kg of grain for a 20 litre batch at typical homebrew efficiency. For a dark table beer, swap the caramel malt for a small amount of a dark Belgian-style caramel malt or a little dark candi syrup, the flavour you would recognise from a dubbel but much lighter.

Mash at about 68 to 69 °C. A warmer mash favours the enzyme that leaves some unfermentable sugars behind, so the beer finishes at a slightly higher final gravity and feels fuller. Aim for a finish around 1.008 to 1.010.

Boil for 60 minutes as usual. Bitterness should be gentle, about 15 to 20 IBU from a noble or English hop added early. Too much bitterness in a light beer quickly tastes harsh because there is so little malt to balance it.

Keep an eye on sparging. With such a small grist you will collect a lot of thin wort at the end. Over-sparging pulls tannin from the husks. Stop collecting when the run-off falls below about 1.010.

The yeast is where a table beer gets its Belgian voice. A Belgian ale or saison strain gives pear, pepper and clove. At this low gravity the yeast has an easy job and finishes quickly, often in four or five days.

Ferment around 20 to 22 °C and let it rise a couple of degrees at the end. In an Indian summer you may struggle to keep it that cool. Wrap the fermenter in a wet towel in front of a fan, or use a cooler box with frozen water bottles changed twice a day. A table beer fermented at 30 °C turns solventy and loses the subtle fruit.

Belgian beers are usually lively. A table beer benefits from it. Aim for about 2.5 to 2.8 volumes of CO2 by bottle conditioning with priming sugar. Bubbles add a sense of fullness that the alcohol cannot.

Serve at 6 to 8 °C in a tumbler or small goblet, with food. Table beer was never meant for a tasting flight. Try it with dosa, khichdi or a simple dal and rice, where its low bitterness and fruit sit comfortably beside the meal.

The common failures are a thin, watery beer from a cool mash, a harsh beer from too many hops or a solventy beer from warm fermentation. Each one comes from treating a small beer like a scaled-down big one.

Designing low strength beer that tastes complete is a style skill in itself. It means knowing how each malt, mash rest and yeast choice adds to body, plus how far to push it before the beer stops tasting Belgian.
faqs: What ABV is a Belgian table beer?
Usually between about 2.5 and 4% ABV. Older versions could be even lower, since they were family beers for everyday meals.
Can I make a table beer from the second runnings of a strong beer?
Yes. Traditional brewers did exactly this, using the weaker last runnings after making a stronger beer. You will need to measure gravity and add a little extract or sugar if it is too low.
Why does my low alcohol beer taste watery?
Usually the mash was too cool, the grist had no body-building malts or carbonation was low. Mash warmer, add wheat or oats and carbonate more.
Which yeast should I use for table beer?
Any Belgian ale or saison strain works. Choose one whose flavour you enjoy, because at this strength the yeast character carries the beer.
